newsitem.title: FINLAND: Upturn seen in European paper despite weak pulp.
newsitem.headline: Upturn seen in European paper despite weak pulp.

text.p: Pulp prices -- the leading indicator for the forest industry business cycle -- remain depressed, but other factors suggest that the European paper market is recovering, analysts said on Wednesday.

With a view to higher profits for Europe's top paper makers in the Nordic countries in 1998, and some help from the dollar's strength, stock markets have recently given leading paper stocks a boost, and analysts believe there is scope for more.
"Our opinion is that it is still worth playing this game," said Carnegie analyst Karri Alameri.
With the expected upturn now lacking the traditional key ingredient of rising pulp prices, some investors are hesitant.
Usually, a sawn goods recovery -- which came last summer -- must be followed by higher pulp prices to gradually prompt higher paper prices, but this time, the marching order has changed.
"What you see now is quite odd for the forest industry. The normal price development of the sector has been turned upside down," said Den Danske Bank forestry analyst Niels Leth.

Europe's largest paper maker UPM-Kymmene -- which on Tuesday reported a sharp fall in 1996 profits and expected a flat performance this year -- forecast falling pulp prices but said it planned to up magazine and fine paper prices this month.

UPM expects the benchmark Northern Bleached Softwood Kraft (NBKS) pulp price to decline in the next few months at a pace of some $1 to $2 per month. An international index compiled in Finland put it at some $540 per tonne on Monday.

Pulp prices are pressured by a break-up of high pulp stocks accumulated last year, and production has remained high, particularly in North America where it is almost impossible to run down pulp mills in the winter, analysts said.
But they saw many encouraging signs.
"Profits will rise in 1998," said Opstock analyst Jukka Linden. This year would be flat for papermakers, with volumes up while average prices would be below last year's, he added.
Paper machine capacity utilisation this year has been strong, and UPM said on Tuesday its hopes of raising prices were based on improving demand.
Since early February, Swedish and Finnish forest industry stock indices have risen 16 percent while the U.S. paper stock index has only inched up two percent.

Analysts said Nordic forest industry shares should be valued lower than markets overall due their cyclical sensitivity, but if one assumes 1996 and 1997 will be the bottom of this cycle and 1998 a recovery, they said current discounts are too high.

Analysts are discounting 1997 and focusing on 1998 prospective price-to-earnings ratios -- at Opstock, eight-nine for UPM compared to about 11 for the Swedish forest industry average. The Helsinki stock exchange average for 1998 is about 11 and Stockholm trades some 20 percent over Helsinki.

Since the expected upturn is already looking irregular, investors may not want to use traditional stockpicking methods -- first buying early cyclical forestry shares and then moving on as the cycle matures, Den Danske's Leth said.

While he in September expected such early cyclical shares as Swedish SCA, MoDo and Finnish Enso to be in early focus, looking at the anomaly of rising late-cycle prices and weak pulp has changed his view.
He now says the trend in particular favours UPM which is big in magazine papers, newsprint and fine papers.
And he recommends switching to Finland from Sweden.
"There is no reason for the Finnish (forestries) to be priced 30 to 40 percent lower than the Swedes," Leth said.
He said the change in the forest industry cycle was driven by Europe's economic trends as austerity ahead of economic and monetary union leads to slower but steadier growth.
